title: Fractional & Small Interests
metaTitle: Selling a Small Fractional Mineral Interest in West Virginia
metaDescription: Own a tiny undivided share of West Virginia mineral rights split among many heirs? We work directly with fractional owners the field-scale buyers pass over.
heroLead: Four generations of intestate succession can turn one tract into forty owners, and most of those owners hold a decimal so small it barely shows up on a division order.
intro: West Virginia has some of the most fragmented mineral ownership in Appalachia, a direct result of land passing through families for a century without formal probate at every generation. A single original tract can end up split among dozens of heirs, each holding an undivided fractional interest measured in ten-thousandths of an acre or less. Those owners often receive royalty checks so small the mailing cost nearly exceeds the payment, and the operator's own records may only have a partial, outdated list of who the current owners actually are.

We buy these small fractional interests directly. The title work is more involved than a single-owner tract, but the process for you as the seller is the same: we confirm your share through the recorded chain, make an offer against that specific fraction, and close.

sections.heading: How a tract fragments across generations
paragraphs: A typical pattern starts with one original mineral owner who died intestate, splitting the interest among several children under West Virginia's descent and distribution rules. Each of those children's shares splits again at the next generation, and by the third or fourth generation an original whole interest can be divided into dozens of fractional shares, some owned by people who have never lived in West Virginia and may not know the interest exists.

The operator's division order department usually only catches up with a fraction of this fragmentation, working from whatever probate or affidavit paperwork was actually filed. That's why some heirs receive regular royalty checks while a sibling holding an identical-sized share receives nothing, simply because their branch of the family never recorded the transfer.

sections.heading: Why small interests are hard to sell to a typical buyer
paragraphs: Most mineral buyers set a minimum transaction size, because the title work and closing cost on a fractional interest is roughly the same whether the interest is large or tiny. A share worth a few hundred dollars a year in royalty, or nothing at all if the tract is unleased, often isn't worth a large buyer's time even though it's very real property with real value to the owner holding it.

We take a different approach because we specialize in exactly this kind of fragmented West Virginia ownership. We're comfortable buying a one-thirty-second interest in forty acres if the chain of title supports it, and we frequently buy several heirs' shares in the same tract in a single closing window.

sections.heading: Confirming your specific fraction before we quote anything
paragraphs: The starting point is always the document that put the interest in your name, a deed, a will, or an affidavit of heirship recorded at the county clerk's office. From there we trace forward to confirm your current fractional share and check whether it matches what the operator has on file. If there's a mismatch, that usually means a prior generation's transfer was never properly recorded, which we can often resolve with an heirship affidavit rather than a full probate proceeding.

This confirmation step protects you as much as it protects a buyer. We won't quote a number until we know exactly what fraction we're valuing, because a decimal error on a small interest changes the offer by a meaningful percentage even when the dollar amount looks small.

sections.heading: What a small-interest closing actually looks like
paragraphs: For most small fractional sales, the paperwork is a straightforward mineral deed conveying your specific share, recorded at the county clerk's office the same as any other real property transfer. We cover recording costs and standard closing costs, and we can typically close within a few weeks of confirming your title, faster if the ownership documentation is already clean.

faqs.question: Is my interest too small to sell?
faqs.answer: Usually not to us. We regularly buy fractional interests down to very small decimals, since we're set up to handle the fragmented ownership common across West Virginia mineral tracts.

faqs.question: I've never received a royalty check. Do I still own something?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Not receiving a check often means the operator's records haven't caught up with your branch of the family, not that your interest doesn't exist. We can check the recorded chain to confirm.

faqs.question: How do you figure out exactly what fraction I own?
faqs.answer: We trace the deed or probate record that established the original interest, then follow it forward through however many generations of heirs, confirming your specific share through recorded documents rather than family recollection alone.

faqs.question: Can you buy interests from several heirs in the same family at once?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it's common. When multiple siblings or cousins hold shares in the same original tract, we can often close all of them in the same window, which simplifies the paperwork for everyone.

faqs.question: What if my share was never formally recorded after a relative died?
faqs.answer: We can often work from an heirship affidavit rather than requiring a full probate proceeding, depending on how the estate was handled. We'll tell you specifically what's needed once we see the existing records.
